title: Good Chaps, Golden Triangles, and the Case for a Written Constitution
label: 16 September 2026 · Lord Case on constitutional safeguards
summary: Lord Case, former Cabinet Secretary and Head of the Civil Service, told the Constitution Committee that the Cabinet Secretary is a tier-two constitutional guardian who advises the Prime Minister and supports the golden triangle of advisers linking No. 10, the Cabinet Office, and the Royal Household. He described how he handled the prospect of Boris Johnson calling a general election to save his premiership by invoking the Lascelles principles, and argued that reliance on unwritten convention and the 'good chaps' theory is inadequate. He called for more codification, ideally a written constitution, and warned that the monarchy is a weak safeguard in extreme circumstances.

speakers.label: Lord Case
speakers.name: Lord Case
speakers.role: Former Cabinet Secretary and Head of the Civil Service, UK Government

chapters.title: The Cabinet Secretary as a tier-two guardian
chapters.takeaway: Lord Case says the Cabinet Secretary advises the PM on constitutional matters but is not the ultimate guardian—the monarch and PM are the tier-one principals.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Lord Case, welcome. We are looking at the UK's constitutional safeguards. What is the Cabinet Secretary's role in the constitution? Would you call the Cabinet Secretary a constitutional guardian?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Good morning. I'd describe the Cabinet Secretary as a tier-two guardian, not tier one. The tier-one guardians are the monarch, the Prime Minister, and maybe one or two others.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: The Cabinet Secretary, the PM's principal private secretary, and the sovereign's private secretary don't have much separate legal status of their own. The serious entities are their principals—the sovereign and the Prime Minister. We're the support cast.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: In practice, the Cabinet Secretary predominantly advises the Prime Minister on constitutional matters. In extremes, you might be drawn into conversations with the sovereign or, more likely, the sovereign's private secretary.

chapters.title: Navigating crises and the 'good chaps' problem
chapters.takeaway: Lord Case says handling four PMs, a pandemic, and a potential election call required trust and precedent—but the informal 'good chaps' model is inadequate for a modern G7 state.

turns.speaker: Baroness Laing of Elderslie
turns.text: You navigated four Prime Ministers in quick succession, plus a pandemic and devolution strains. What can we learn from that?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: The lessons are mostly about internal party operation, not the constitution. At the heart is a trusting relationship with key colleagues and access to predecessors.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: A good example: when Boris Johnson's Cabinet was collapsing, someone around him floated calling a general election to avoid him being brought down by his own party.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: I had to get out the Lascelles principles and the 1950 'Senex' letter, show them, and say: here's why that's a bad idea and why the sovereign might be within their rights to refuse. Don't pursue that line.

turns.speaker: Baroness Laing of Elderslie
turns.text: So the Cabinet Secretary has to have the theory, access to predecessors, and the strength to stand up to an outspoken Cabinet Minister who thinks public opinion is on his side?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Yes. You need to be confident of your ground—what are facts, what is your judgment, what is opinion—and willing to explain that to a PM or Cabinet Minister.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: It can be lonely. Having predecessors to consult and good relationships with critical colleagues, like the sovereign's private secretary, is essential.

turns.speaker: Baroness Laing of Elderslie
turns.text: So there's an informal body of experienced people forming a guardianship of the constitution?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: I'd say so—but I think it's inadequate. I started as a PhD student under Lord Hennessy celebrating our unwritten constitution, but I've become convinced we should head towards a more codified, written constitution.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: I loathe the phrase 'good chaps' to describe this. Historically, nearly all these guardians were chaps—same schools, same universities, same social class. That isn't a justifiable way to manage a 21st-century G7 economy.

chapters.title: Trust, confidentiality, and weaknesses of the role
chapters.takeaway: The Cabinet Secretary's effectiveness depends on trust and confidentiality, but he can be hired and fired by the PM—a structural weakness when constitutional advice is ignored.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: At its heart is trust, confidentiality, and knowledge. The tier-twos need a relationship. Lord Young emphasised the private nature of monarch-PM conversations. Presumably the Cabinet Secretary also needs to hold deeply private discussions with the PPSs?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Absolutely essential. Just as there's confidentiality and trust upstairs between the PM and sovereign, exactly the same has to be going on downstairs.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: That's one reason rapid turnover of PPSs and Cabinet Secretaries is a bad idea. It's particularly bad for forming the trusted relationships that matter when the constitutional chips are down.

turns.speaker: Lord Beith
turns.text: Did you have to educate Prime Ministers on constitutional principles they were unfamiliar with?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Yes. Despite many having been to the nation's finest schools and universities, it turned out some bits of their education had been missing.

turns.speaker: Lord Murphy of Torfaen
turns.text: Does the Cabinet Secretary have weaknesses as a constitutional guardian? If you couldn't persuade a PM that something was fundamentally wrong, at what point would you resign?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Inherent weaknesses, yes. You're appointed and dismissed at the will of the Prime Minister. If the PM ignores your advice, in extremis they could dismiss you and bring in someone who'll give different advice.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: The Cabinet Secretary could say: 'You're not listening. This isn't a policy judgment; it's a critical point of constitutional safety. I'm going to resign.' You could imagine that.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Lord O'Donnell said if something was illegal that was helpful—you could say 'PM, that's illegal.' But where it's not illegal yet constitutionally extremely difficult, the final position is resignation, which itself could trigger a constitutional crisis.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: That's right. Though in modern politics, I'm not sure a Cabinet Secretary's resignation would have that impact. We come and go like London buses now. It depends on personalities and context.

turns.speaker: Lord Murphy of Torfaen
turns.text: There's a difference between being sacked and saying 'I'm going because you're making a major constitutional mistake' and making sure the world knows. Wouldn't that have an impact?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: It would, but it depends on personalities and context. That's exactly why we need to codify these things. Leaving it to the chance of a Cabinet Secretary resigning and making the right fuss feels like an unreliable way to alert the nation to something constitutionally unwise.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Lord Young distinguished something in a newly elected Government's manifesto that was constitutionally offensive—much harder to block. You agree?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: I couldn't agree more. That's the great challenge for anyone unelected. If the PM, supported by Cabinet and Parliament, is carrying out a manifesto commitment, the unelected pretty much have to get out of the way.

chapters.title: Codification and the case for a written constitution
chapters.takeaway: Lord Case favours moving key conventions into legislation and, ultimately, a written constitution—but accepts it would take a major crisis to achieve.

turns.speaker: Lord Burnett of Maldon
turns.text: You've said you're convinced we need a more codified constitution. Are you thinking of putting conventions into legislation, or something more radical like a formal written constitution?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Personally, I'm at the more radical end. But I'm a pragmatist—it'll be a long time until we have a written constitution. Nations only get one out of extreme circumstances. We're not there yet.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: A pragmatic approach is needed. Look at the Cabinet Manual—it's woefully out of date. I produced an updated draft three or four PMs ago. All said they'd publish it, but it hasn't been done. It's crazy.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: The Cabinet Manual has no authority or effect. It just sits there. Some aspects might be worth bringing into legislation.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: One specific example: a requirement to have a Deputy Prime Minister. After the episode where Boris Johnson could have needed a ventilator, we put arrangements in place to always have one. The Covid inquiry agreed.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: But the current Prime Minister hasn't appointed one. It was still totally open to a new PM to say 'No thanks.' For the safety and certainty of managing the nation, we shouldn't leave that to the whim of a PM.

chapters.title: The golden triangle and the monarch's role
chapters.takeaway: The golden triangle is a network of advisers, not principals, and in a crisis it goes on alert to share information—but the monarch remains a weak safeguard in extreme scenarios.

turns.speaker: Lord Cryer
turns.text: What role does the PM's principal private secretary play in constitutional decision-making?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: It's the least understood corner of the golden triangle. The PM's PPS is the much more frequent conduit between Government and the sovereign—talking several times a week about what's going on, delivering a 'no surprises' approach.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: It's not about grand crises every week. It's the flow of information about what's on the PM's mind, military campaigns, Parliament. Cabinet Secretary interactions are fewer—usually when you're crossing the threshold of a serious constitutional issue.

turns.speaker: Lord Cryer
turns.text: On 'no surprises,' you said a system was established to ensure PMs appoint a Deputy PM, but it hasn't happened. Historically the Leader of the House was seen as number two. Now we have a First Secretary, Louise Haigh, but it's still in doubt who'd take over.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: I completely agree. We're a $4 trillion economy, a nuclear power, a P5 nation—you and I shouldn't be sitting here making assumptions about who's in charge if the PM is unavailable. Come on.

turns.speaker: Lord Bellamy
turns.text: You said anyone unelected has to get out of the way. What if a Government has a narrow majority but a minority of the popular vote, with a fragmented party scene? Does that change things?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: The principle remains the same. If you're unelected, you must be extremely conscious of that and recognise you're ultimately secondary to any elected Government.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Before the sovereign exercises prerogative powers, an unelected figure would need to be very sure of the ground and take very broad advice, making sure they have support from important people.

turns.speaker: Lord Bellamy
turns.text: Does it follow that the monarchy as such is quite a weak constitutional safeguard in extreme circumstances?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: In my view, yes.

turns.speaker: Lord Burnett of Maldon
turns.text: The golden triangle so far seems to lubricate an engine that's working well. How should it operate if the engine is breaking down?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Historically, 1974, it operated by walks around St James's Park—still important. More seriously, in those days at the end of Boris Johnson's time, as soon as the election idea came to me, I was on the phone to other members of the golden triangle.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: I said: 'There's something happening here. We need to step up our golden triangle DEFCON level. We need to communicate a lot. Stand on alert.'

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: The primary task is exchange of information and triangulation of advice: 'This is what I'm saying to the PM,' 'This is what I'm saying to the sovereign.' Make sure the facts and precedents are consistent.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: But the golden triangle are advisers. We've elevated it in some constitutional fantasy league, but the reality is all members are advisers to principals. They're not principals themselves.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You described tier-one and tier-two guardians. You said the monarch as a safeguard is weaker. Would you strengthen it? Or is the real backstop in Whitehall or Parliament?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: I would not strengthen the monarch's role. In a 21st-century democracy, strengthening an unelected Head of State goes against the flow of our history.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: The strength of the backstop leads me to conclude that the best backstop is probably a written constitution. It certainly shouldn't be in the hands of anyone in Whitehall. Gatekeepers like Cabinet Secretaries are important, but ultimately these things need to rest in settled law.

chapters.title: Strengthening safeguards short of a written constitution
chapters.takeaway: Lord Case suggests moving critical conventions into legislation and removing ambiguities about succession, while acknowledging a written constitution would need a major crisis to achieve.

turns.speaker: Lord Murphy of Torfaen
turns.text: Isn't there a contradiction? You argue for a written constitution, where the monarch's role would be defined in writing, but the strength of the present situation is that it's not defined in writing.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: It's a wonderful essay question. I learned under Peter Hennessy to celebrate the glories and flexibility of our unwritten constitution. But seeing it up close, and questions about transparency, who wields power, in whose interests, and how you get rid of them—those have led me to think a written constitution might be the right answer.

turns.speaker: Lord Jones of Penybont
turns.text: I operated within a written constitution in devolved Wales—four founding Acts of Parliament. It works pretty well. But I'm pragmatic enough to know a written constitution isn't around the corner. Short of that, is there anything that could strengthen our safeguards?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Identifying critical things we might move from precedent or the Cabinet Manual into legislation feels like a good idea.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: There's an enormously significant constitutional change happening now—allowing a Roman Catholic or Jewish Prime Minister to be involved in appointing Church of England bishops. What on earth is that about? It's a significant historical move.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: More seriously, I'd look at questions around order of precedence— who do you call if X or Y is unavailable? We should take away the ambiguity and assumptions Lord Cryer and I discussed. You wouldn't run a business like that, so why run a country with this uncertainty?

turns.speaker: Baroness Hamwee
turns.text: Is the constitution overall vulnerable, and in what ways?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Over recent years, we've seen an amazing amount of freedom for a Government to ignore precedent and ignore advice drawn from the 'good faith' theory. It feels like a growing trend.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Things that used to be pencil lines in and around our constitution perhaps should be turned into inked lines. Even with a written constitution, personality and context will always be critical. I'm not naive about politics.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Leo Amery described the constitution as 'a living structure, continuously shaped in the course of history by the interaction of individual purposes and collective instincts with the requirements of ever-varying circumstances.' It's wonderful.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: But should we really be operating a 21st-century G7, P5, nuclear-armed state in that way? It would be good to have a few more inked lines.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hamwee
turns.text: Getting from here to there—would aiming for a written constitution gum up everything else?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: It would be extremely difficult as part of normal politics. You shift to a written constitution coming out of very large-scale national or international crisis—liberation moments. I'm highly pragmatic about how you'd get there.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Look at House of Lords reform: the moment you go into that, it can gum everything up. I'd be very cautious about jumping all the way to a written constitution through normal times of Parliament.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. We're trying to look ahead 10 to 15 years at constitutional weaknesses and whether we need to strengthen safeguards. Anything else you'd like to finish on?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: No. Thank you very much. More power to your elbow.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thanks a lot. I now draw this session to a close.
